Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run from a script) to finish the whole pipeline yourself.  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, show the exact shell commands, and illustrate how to use the two helper functions (`create_a_docker_file` and `create_kubernetes_yaml_file`) that were supplied in the prompt.  

> **NOTE** – I don’t have the ability to actually clone the repo or push commits from here, so the instructions assume you’re running them locally on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and the `functions` module available.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Inspect the Repo

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
tree -L 2   # shows top‑level directories/files
cat package.json   # look at dependencies, scripts, etc.
```

Typical findings for a minimal Node.js project:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `app.js` | Main entry point |
| `package.json` | Dependencies + start script |
| `.env.example` | Sample environment variables |

Assume the app listens on port `3000`.

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Use the provided function:

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    base_image="node:18-alpine", # lightweight Node runtime
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint="node app.js"
)
```

This writes a `Dockerfile` similar to:

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> If you already had a Dockerfile, replace it with this one or merge the relevant parts.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAMLs

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

Resulting `k8s.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Adjust `image_name` to match your registry and tag strategy.

### 2.4 Add a GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> Replace `your-dockerhub-username` with your actual Docker Hub account.  
> Store `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` as repository secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you want to stage everything automatically:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` accordingly.

---

## Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile generated |
| ✅ | Kubernetes YAML generated |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow added |
| ✅ | Files staged |
| ✅ | Commit made |
| ✅ | Pushed to remote |

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next commit to `main`. It will build the image, cache layers, and push it to Docker Hub. You can then deploy to a cluster with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

Happy coding!
